faq.q: Is there an entrance exam or interview?
faq.a: It depends on the programme. Many programmes require an online entrance test, a written assignment or an interview, especially for competitive or research-based fields. These assess your academic readiness and, for doctoral applicants, the strength of your research plan, so prepare to discuss your field and motivation clearly.

posts.title: IELTS 7+ in 6 Weeks: A Realistic IELTS Study Plan
posts.metaDescription: A realistic 6-week IELTS study plan to reach Band 7+. Week-by-week schedule, section strategies, and practice routines for busy applicants.
posts.excerpt: A week-by-week IELTS study plan that takes you from your current level to a Band 7 or higher in six focused weeks, with section-specific strategies and honest expectations.
posts.bodyHtml:
Can I reach Band 7 in six weeks?

Yes, if you already test at roughly Band 6 to 6.5 and can study consistently. This IELTS study plan gives you a realistic, week-by-week route to the score rather than vague advice to practise more. It assumes roughly 1.5 to 2 hours on weekdays and a longer block at weekends. If your current level is closer to Band 5, use this as a strong foundation and plan on extending the timeline.

What makes this IELTS study plan realistic?

A useful IELTS study plan is not designed to teach English from scratch. Its job is to teach you the test, close specific skill gaps, and build the stamina required to perform for nearly three hours. Band 7 rewards accuracy, range, and control, so fluent conversation alone is not enough.

Key takeaways

What are the most important takeaways?

  • Band 7 in six weeks is realistic if you start around Band 6 to 6.5 and study consistently.
  • Take a full timed diagnostic test before you plan anything, so your IELTS study plan targets real weaknesses.
  • Writing and Speaking are where most people lose marks; they need active feedback, not passive practice.
  • Reading and Listening improve fastest through timed practice plus error analysis.
  • Simulate full test conditions in the final two weeks to build stamina and reduce exam-day surprises.

Understand what Band 7 actually requires

How is my overall IELTS band calculated?

Each of the four sections is scored from 0 to 9, and your overall result is the average, rounded to the nearest half band. To reach an overall 7, you generally need scores of about 6.5 to 7.5 across the board, so one weak section can pull the total down. Many universities also impose a minimum score in every section, making balance more useful than one exceptional result.

What does a Band 7 performance look like?

Band 7 descriptors reward clear, measurable behaviours. In Writing, you need clear organisation, varied sentence structures, and only occasional errors. In Speaking, you need fluency without long pauses, flexible vocabulary, and generally accurate grammar. Once you understand those standards, your IELTS study plan becomes a sequence of targeted improvements rather than guesswork.

Choose Academic or General Training early

Most university and scholarship applicants take the Academic version. Listening and Speaking are the same in both versions, but Reading and Writing differ. Confirm that you are booked for Academic before spending six weeks practising the wrong Task 1 if your goal is study or a scholarship.

Week 0: The diagnostic weekend

Why should I take a diagnostic test first?

Before Week 1, sit one complete official practice test under timed conditions. Do not pause, look up words, or give yourself extra minutes. This is the most valuable hour of the entire IELTS study plan because it shows your real starting point before targets and study time can be assigned.

How should I score and record the diagnostic?

Mark the test honestly. Convert your Reading and Listening raw totals into band scores. For Writing and Speaking, compare your performance with the public band descriptors, or obtain feedback from a teacher or reliable assessment tool. Record four numbers, one for each section, because that baseline will determine what every later session should prioritise.

Weeks 1 to 2: Build accuracy and fix the basics

How should I balance work in the first fortnight?

Turn your diagnosis into action. Alternate Reading and Listening on different days, schedule Writing twice a week, and practise Speaking in short daily bursts. This balanced opening phase corrects basic errors before you add speed, pressure, and more advanced language.

How should I improve Listening?

Complete one Listening section each day and always review your mistakes. Common losses come from spelling, plurals, and losing your place when a speaker paraphrases. Predict answers before the audio begins, and keep listening after an error instead of freezing over the answer you missed.

What is the best Reading approach in Weeks 1 and 2?

Prioritise technique over speed at first. Learn to scan for keywords, recognise paraphrase, and handle True/False/Not Given, which can trip up even strong readers. Give each passage 20 minutes so the clock feels normal from the beginning rather than becoming a crisis later.

How much Writing should I complete?

Write one Task 1 and one Task 2 during the fortnight, but analyse model answers more deeply than you simply produce extra essays. Study the structure of a Band 7 essay: a clear position, two developed body paragraphs, and a conclusion. For Academic Task 1, begin building a reliable bank of phrases for trends, comparisons, and processes.

How can I improve Speaking every day?

Record yourself answering Part 1 questions each day and listen back for hesitation, repetition, and abrupt endings. Even two minutes of self-recording exposes habits that you cannot notice while speaking in the moment. Use the recordings to make your next answer more fluent and more precise.

Weeks 3 to 4: Expand range and add pressure

What should change in Weeks 3 and 4?

By now, the format should feel familiar, so use the middle phase to expand range. Work on more sophisticated vocabulary, more varied grammar, and faster processing. Move Reading and Listening to complete timed sections, and increase the amount of feedback you receive on Writing.

How should I grow vocabulary in context?

Do not memorise isolated word lists. Collect contextual vocabulary around common IELTS themes such as education, environment, technology, health, and urban life. For each theme, record five collocations that you can actually use in an essay or Speaking answer. Range with control is more valuable than rare words used incorrectly.

How should I target Writing Task 2?

Give Task 2 the most attention because it carries more weight than Task 1. Write two fully timed 40-minute essays each week. After each one, ask whether you answered the exact question, whether every paragraph develops one idea, and whether your sentence structures vary. Grammatical range and accuracy accounts for 25 percent of the Writing score, so deliberately combine simple, compound, and complex sentences.

The fastest way to lose a Writing band is to write a memorised essay that does not address the specific question. Examiners are trained to spot this instantly.

How can I build Speaking stamina?

Move to full Part 2 long turns. Use the one-minute preparation period to jot down keywords, then speak for the entire two minutes without stopping. If your ideas run dry, add an example, a contrast, or a short personal story. Fluency includes stamina, and two minutes feels difficult until you have practised it repeatedly.

Weeks 5 to 6: Simulate, refine, and peak

How should I use full mock tests?

Sit two full timed mock tests, ideally at weekends, in one sitting with realistic breaks. The final fortnight should focus on performance rather than new learning. This concentration drill is what separates a genuine Band 7 performance from a candidate who scores well on isolated sections but fades during the real test.

What should I repair between mocks?

Spend the time between mocks repairing only your weakest area. If Listening Part 4 repeatedly costs marks, drill that part. If Writing coherence is weak, rewrite two older essays with better linking. Avoid spending most of your time on comfortable strengths merely because practising them feels more pleasant.

How should I plan my exam-day routine?

Set section-by-section timings in advance. Reading usually needs 20 minutes per passage, and you should never leave a blank answer. For Writing, allow about 20 minutes for Task 1 and 40 for Task 2, then use the final five minutes to check slips. Rehearsing this routine removes difficult decisions from the actual exam.

Section strategies that reliably add marks

What should I do during Listening?

Read the questions before each recording and underline keywords. Watch for distractors in which a speaker mentions a wrong answer before correcting it. Transfer your answers carefully, and never leave a blank because there is no penalty for guessing.

What should I do during Reading?

Do not read every word. Skim for the text structure, then scan for the information that each question specifically requests. Control your pace so one passage cannot take minutes needed by another, and remember that most questions follow the order of information in the text.

What should I do before and during Writing?

Plan for two minutes before you begin. A short plan prevents the mid-answer drift that damages coherence. Use clear paragraphs, natural linking devices, and precise vocabulary, then reserve time to proofread articles, plurals, subject-verb agreement, and verb tenses.

How should I approach Speaking Part 2?

Extend every answer with a reason and an example. Treat the examiner as a curious conversation partner rather than an interrogator. It is acceptable to correct yourself, and a natural pause to think sounds much better than repeated filler noise.

How to know your plan is working

How should I track progress across six weeks?

Record your mock band scores throughout the six weeks. Expect steady but uneven improvement: Reading and Listening often rise first because they respond quickly to deliberate practice, while Writing and Speaking usually move more slowly because they depend on feedback and changed habits. If a score remains flat for two weeks, change the method instead of repeating the same ineffective routine.

How is IELTS preparation connected to my application?

The same discipline that improves your IELTS result will strengthen the rest of your application. If you are comparing universities and funding at the same time, our scholarship results tool can help you shortlist programmes that match your profile, while our AI advisor can help sanity-check whether your target band satisfies each course requirement.

IELTS 7+ in 6 Weeks: A Realistic IELTS Study Plan: what this guide covers

Who is this IELTS study plan designed for?

This guide explains what a Pakistani student needs to know about an IELTS study plan, including the goals, resources, timelines, and practical preparation steps involved. Use the sections above to find the exact information you need, or bookmark this page and return as your test date and application plans develop.

Common mistakes that keep people at Band 6.5

Which mistakes prevent candidates from reaching Band 7?

Three habits stall applicants just short of Band 7. First is passive practice: completing test after test without analysing any errors. Second is memorising essays and answers, which examiners penalise. Third is ignoring one weak section until it quietly caps the overall score. A disciplined IELTS study plan addresses all three by combining practice with reflection and balancing effort across every section.

What should I do to avoid staying at Band 6.5?

Stay consistent, review every mistake, and simulate the real test before exam day. Six focused weeks of that disciplined approach will move most candidates who begin around Band 6.5 into Band 7 territory, provided they respond to feedback and concentrate on their weakest areas.

How to structure your daily IELTS study plan sessions

Why does daily session structure matter?

A week-by-week roadmap is important, but your day-to-day habits determine whether six weeks produce real improvement. A structured IELTS study plan session turns effort into measurable progress; unstructured practice may merely make you familiar with the test format without closing any skill gaps.

How should I organise a 90-minute weekday session?

Divide a productive weekday session of ninety minutes to two hours into three parts. Begin with a warm-up focused on your weakest skill, which for many Pakistani students is Writing Task 2 or Speaking Part 3. Use the first twenty-five minutes to write one timed body paragraph or answer two Part 3 questions aloud, record yourself, and listen back.

What are the IELTS study plan requirements?

The middle section should last about fifty minutes and provide skill-building work on a rotating basis. Alternate Reading and Listening on different days, complete one practice-test section under time, and then spend fifteen minutes examining every error. In Reading, identify whether an error came from vocabulary, a misread question, or time pressure. In Listening, replay the relevant audio and write exactly what you missed.

How should I consolidate vocabulary and grammar?

Use the final twenty minutes for vocabulary and grammar consolidation. Keep a notebook divided by IELTS topic, including education, health, environment, and technology. After each session, record three to five useful words or phrases and write one original sentence using each. Review the notebook at the start of every session; spaced repetition builds the range that separates a Band 6 writer from a Band 7 writer.

What should a weekend session include?

Make weekend sessions three to four hours when possible. Take one full timed practice test in the morning and review it thoroughly in the afternoon. Sit at a desk, use only permitted materials, follow every section limit strictly, and reproduce the real test's breaks rather than inventing extra time.

Best free and low-cost IELTS resources for Pakistani students

Do I need an expensive IELTS course?

No. High-quality IELTS preparation does not require an expensive course or premium materials. Free and low-cost resources can provide the practice, models, and feedback needed to move towards Band 7 when you use them actively and consistently throughout your IELTS study plan.

Which official practice resources should I prioritise?

The most valuable free resource is IELTS official sample tests. British Council, IDP, and Cambridge publish practice tests that reflect the real question types and difficulty. Complete at least four full official tests during the six-week plan, ideally one per week in Weeks 2 through 5. Accurate official material is far more useful than a large pile of unrelated third-party questions.

What is IELTS study plan?

For listening practice, BBC Learning English and the BBC World Service podcast archive provide useful material at an appropriate level. Focus on science, education, and social issues, which resemble topics in Listening Sections 3 and 4. Listen actively, take notes, summarise what you heard, and check your understanding against a transcript when one is available.

What should you write in your IELTS study plan essays?

For writing, free online feedback platforms can be useful. The British Council IELTS Prepare website provides model answers assessed against official band descriptors. Compare your work paragraph by paragraph and identify the difference between Band 6 and Band 7 writing: more precise vocabulary, varied cohesion devices, and a clear position maintained throughout.

How can I practise Speaking for free?

For speaking, record yourself answering Part 2 cue cards on your phone. Allow one minute to prepare and two uninterrupted minutes to speak. Listen back honestly and ask whether you maintained fluency, used a range of grammar, developed your ideas, and avoided unnecessary repetition.

Where can I find free Reading practice?

For reading, academic articles from The Guardian, The Economist, and New Scientist make useful practice material. Read one article each day under a twenty-minute timer. Identify the main idea, the supporting arguments, and the author's attitude instead of trying to understand every isolated word.

How much does IELTS study plan cost?

Low-cost paid options include Cambridge IELTS practice-test books, which cost approximately two to three thousand rupees and contain four complete tests each. Buy at least two volumes during your preparation period, use the tests progressively, and review each answer before moving on.

Band 7 scoring demands: what each IELTS section actually requires

Why should I learn the section-by-section Band 7 requirements?

Understanding what Band 7 demands in each IELTS section lets you target preparation precisely. It prevents you from spending every week improving general English and hoping an unpredictable score will follow. Your diagnostic should determine how much time each skill receives within the overall IELTS study plan.

What does Listening Band 7 require?

Listening (band 7 = 30 to 31 correct answers out of 40): You need to catch detailed information in academic discussions, follow multi-stage arguments, and identify a speaker's opinion or attitude. A common problem for Pakistani students is pace rather than vocabulary: the audio moves faster than natural conversation at home. Train by listening to academic podcasts at normal speed and taking notes simultaneously.

What does Reading Band 7 require?

Reading (band 7 = 30 to 31 correct answers out of 40): A Band 7 reader follows complex arguments, understands implicit meaning, and identifies main ideas in dense academic texts. True, False, Not Given is often the decisive weakness because it requires separating information contradicted by the text from information the text simply does not provide.

What does Writing Band 7 require?

Writing (band 7 = scored on four criteria): Examiners assess task response, cohesion and coherence, lexical resource, and grammatical range and accuracy. Band 7 requires full task coverage, a clear position, logical organisation, effective paragraphing, sufficiently precise vocabulary, some correct less-common items, and a controlled mix of simple and complex sentences with only occasional errors.

What does Speaking Band 7 require?

Speaking (band 7 = scored on four criteria): You should speak at length without noticeable effort, use discourse markers and some less-common or idiomatic vocabulary, and handle complex structures with good control. Over-reliance on memorised phrases is a major barrier because it limits development and can be detected immediately.

How should I balance uneven section scores?

Once you know the Band 7 standard, identify your exact weaknesses and allocate preparation time accordingly. For example, a candidate at Band 6 in Listening and Band 7.5 in Reading should devote more of Weeks 1 through 4 to Listening drills. This does not mean ignoring strengths; it means preventing a low score from capping the overall result.

How Pakistani students can leverage local study groups for IELTS preparation

Why should I join a local study group?

Solo study has value, but a local group can accelerate progress in ways isolated preparation cannot easily reproduce. Its strongest value is accountability and realistic Speaking practice, while written peer review can also expose weaknesses before they become exam-day surprises.

How can a study group improve Speaking?

The clearest benefit is regular speaking practice with feedback. IELTS Speaking is a face-to-face conversation, so speaking to a mirror or a recording only goes so far. A group of three to five can meet weekly, rotate examiner and candidate roles, and use official cue cards from recent test cycles. After each two-minute turn, give structured feedback on fluency, vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation.

How do you apply for IELTS study plan?

A group also provides accountability. If you commit to reviewing writing every Saturday morning, you are much more likely to complete the week's homework than if only you know your plan. That social commitment sustains momentum during the difficult middle weeks, when personal motivation often falls.

Which IELTS study plan tips actually work?

For the writing section, peer review is especially useful because different writers approach the same prompt in different ways. Have four people answer one Task 2 question and exchange essays. Use a fixed review order—task response, coherence, vocabulary, then grammar—to mirror the official scoring criteria and make feedback consistent.

How can I find study-group members in Pakistan?

Look through university English departments, coaching centres, and local Facebook groups for IELTS candidates. A group of four or five people from different universities often works well because members bring different perspectives, experience levels, and English-language backgrounds. Choose people who attend consistently and offer honest feedback rather than those who merely want company.

What rules should an IELTS study group set?

Agree at the beginning to meet at a fixed time and place, complete assigned work before each meeting, and give feedback that is honest but constructive. Clear expectations turn an informal gathering into a useful support system. A well-run group can be the difference between repeatedly scoring Band 6.5 and breaking through to Band 7.

A week-by-week practice test schedule for the six-week IELTS 7.0 plan

How should I schedule practice tests?

Practice tests are the backbone of serious IELTS preparation, but random tests waste their diagnostic and training value. A planned schedule gives every test a specific purpose at the correct stage of your six-week IELTS study plan.

What should I do in Week 1?

Week 1 (diagnostic): Complete one full official practice test under strict timed conditions and immediately record an estimated band for each section. Treat this as your baseline, then focus weekday sessions on your two weakest sections.

What should I do in Week 2?

Week 2 (accuracy focus): Do not take another full test. Complete individual sections from a second test, one per day, initially without time pressure so you can focus on accuracy. Record every wrong answer and label its cause: a misread question, vocabulary gap, careless error, or time pressure.

What should I do in Week 3?

Week 3 (timed sections): Complete a full Listening test and a full Reading test under timed conditions. Finish both Writing tasks within the official sixty minutes. Track how long each task takes and note where you begin to run out of time.

What should I do in Week 4?

Week 4 (full test under pressure): Take a complete practice test under strict exam conditions, with no phone, dictionary, or extra breaks. Score it and compare the result with the Week 1 baseline. Aim to improve by at least half a band in your weakest section, even if the overall gain is smaller.

What should I do in Week 5?

Week 5 (refinement): Take another complete test, but spend most of the review on answers that were correct yet uncertain. Eliminating near-misses can move you from Band 6.5 to Band 7. Review Writing and Speaking against the official band descriptors as well.

What should I do in Week 6?

Week 6 (peak simulation): Take your final full practice test in the first half of the week. Use the second half to review all previous error notebooks, concentrating on recurring patterns instead of learning new material. The objective is confidence in the skills you have already established.

Common time traps in the IELTS exam that keep candidates below band 7

What time traps cause avoidable score losses?

Many candidates who understand English well enough for Band 7 lose marks through preventable time-management errors, not a lack of language ability. Once you can name each trap, you can rehearse a specific response before the real test.

How should I manage Reading time?

In IELTS Reading, the most damaging trap is reading every word from beginning to end. The test contains roughly 2,500 words across three passages, but only sixty minutes are available. Strong Band 7 candidates skim the structure first, then use keyword scanning to locate the exact information each question requires.

What IELTS study plan tips should you follow?

In IELTS Listening, the main trap is remaining stuck on a missed question. If the audio continues while you rethink the previous answer, you can lose the next several questions. Write your best guess, mark the item, and move forward. Use the transfer time at the end of a section to revisit marked questions.

How do I avoid the Task 1 time trap?

In IELTS Writing Task 1, candidates can waste time describing individual data points rather than identifying major patterns. Task 1 tests selective summary and comparison, not transcription. Spend three to four minutes finding two or three major trends, then write a structured overview and grouped details in approximately fifteen to eighteen minutes.

How much space should Task 2 receive?

In IELTS Writing Task 2, an overlong introduction and underdeveloped body can leave no room for a proper conclusion or fully developed argument. A Band 7 response usually has a two- or three-sentence introduction, two coherent body paragraphs of six to eight sentences, and a concise two-sentence conclusion. Develop ideas rather than padding sentences.

How should I manage energy in Speaking?

In IELTS Speaking, giving overly long answers to Part 1 can use up mental energy before the more demanding Parts 2 and 3. Keep Part 1 responses to two or three sentences. Save fuller explanations, examples, and analysis for the two-minute long turn and the abstract questions that follow.

How to stay motivated during the six-week IELTS preparation period

How can I stay motivated for six weeks?

Motivation naturally fluctuates during intensive preparation, and most candidates underestimate that challenge. Initial enthusiasm often fades around Week 3, exactly when steady work matters most. Build motivation strategies into the IELTS study plan from the beginning so the mid-cycle dip does not derail your progress.

How does visual progress tracking help?

The first strategy is visual progress tracking. After each practice test, record every estimated section score on a chart or spreadsheet. An upward trend provides concrete evidence that your work is producing results. When motivation is low, reviewing that evidence reminds you why the daily IELTS study plan sessions are worth completing.

How does the IELTS study plan application work?

The second strategy is reward-based milestones. Set a specific weekly goal and attach a modest reward to it. For example, complete all sessions in Week 2 and reach at least Band 6.5 in a practice test before treating yourself to something enjoyable. Achievable rewards make progress tangible and keep the larger Band 7 goal from feeling abstract.

Why does social accountability matter?

The third strategy is social accountability. Tell a friend, relative, or study partner about your plan and ask for occasional check-ins. Knowing that someone is following your progress creates an external commitment that supports motivation. A study group also supplies a useful weekly accountability point without requiring constant self-monitoring.

How can I reinforce my reason for taking IELTS?

The fourth strategy is purpose reinforcement. Remind yourself whether you are working towards a scholarship, admission condition, career goal, or another concrete outcome. Write the reason on a card and keep it where you study. Connecting daily effort to a meaningful long-term goal changes the IELTS study plan from a temporary chore into an investment in your future.

How does variety protect my motivation?

The fifth strategy is variety in practice materials. Repeating the same activity every day quickly becomes monotonous. Alternate official IELTS tests, topics, and skill focuses, and combine practice material with academic articles, podcasts, and suitable online resources. Variation keeps attention active while still testing the same core abilities.

What should I do on a low-motivation day?

Finally, accept that motivation fluctuates. Not wanting to study on some days is normal. Promise yourself only fifteen minutes of light practice, such as reviewing the vocabulary notebook or listening to a short podcast. Starting is often the hardest step, and momentum frequently carries you into a full session. Consistency on difficult days matters more than exceptional intensity on easy ones.

How Pakistani students can use online IELTS communities and forums for preparation

How can online communities support my preparation?

Online communities can supplement an IELTS study plan with free resources, peer encouragement, and current experiences from other candidates. They work best when you use them selectively: gather useful evidence, contribute constructively, and verify advice against official scoring information.

What peer support can I find online?

Platforms such as Reddit, Facebook groups, and dedicated forums offer peer support and shared experiences. Reading about Pakistani students who reached Band 7 in six weeks can provide practical tips and realistic proof that your target is possible. Members may also share study strategies, resource recommendations, and mistakes to avoid.

Can online communities provide materials and feedback?

Yes. Online groups often share free practice materials and feedback, including links to practice tests, model essays, and cue cards. Some run weekly writing submissions with peer comments. This feedback cannot replace professional assessment, but it can reveal clarity, grammar, or structure problems that self-review misses.

How can I find a local study partner online?

Online communities can also connect you with study partners in your city or region. IELTS Facebook groups for Pakistani students often contain requests from learners in Lahore, Karachi, Islamabad, and other cities. A suitable online connection may be more effective than waiting for a partner to appear on a university notice board.

Which online communities should I choose?

Search specifically for IELTS preparation for Pakistani students. Prefer groups with active moderation, regular discussion, questions, and genuinely shared resources. Avoid communities that are mainly promotional or that encourage the distribution of copyrighted practice materials. A smaller active group can be more useful than a huge inactive one.

How should I participate in an online forum?

Contribute as well as consume. Answer another student's question when you can, share your own experience, and give specific, respectful feedback. Explaining a strategy to others exposes gaps in your understanding and builds confidence in what you know. Clear reasoning is more useful than unsupported claims that one method works for everyone.

Should I trust every tip found online?

No, because not all advice in online communities is accurate. IELTS advice varies widely, and some popular tips contradict the official scoring criteria. Verify new strategies against official IELTS resources, assess whether they make logical sense, and test them briefly against your own practice performance before giving them a permanent place in your study routine.

Can online members provide useful test-day information?

Online communities are useful for test-day information. Recent test-takers may describe the centre environment, format updates, arrival procedures, or their experience on the day. This cannot predict actual questions, but it can reduce uncertainty by clarifying logistics and the general conditions you should expect.

What should I do during the final two days?

The last two days are not for new learning. Use them to consolidate familiar material, calm your nerves, and confirm practical arrangements. A busy revision schedule at this stage can increase anxiety without improving your established skills.

What should I do the day before the exam?

On the day before the exam, revise lightly. Read your vocabulary notebook, review the grammar errors identified during six weeks of practice, and skim one or two model essays. Do not take a full test, because a disappointing score this late offers little useful information and may unnecessarily damage your confidence.

What documents do you need for IELTS study plan?

Prepare everything the evening before. Charge your phone if your centre requires a mobile device, and pack your admission ticket, passport or national identity document, water, and permitted stationery. Confirm the exact centre location and travel plan, allowing generous time for traffic and the delays common in busy Pakistani commercial areas.

Why should I organise my test materials early?

Early preparation removes avoidable stress. On test morning, your attention should remain on staying calm and performing, not locating a missing document or worrying that traffic will make you late. A simple checklist and a confirmed route allow you to leave home with confidence.

What should I do on the exam morning?

On the morning of the exam, eat a light meal before leaving home. Arrive at least thirty minutes early to allow for security checks and registration. Trust the preparation you completed, manage each section according to your rehearsed routine, and focus on the question in front of you rather than worrying about earlier answers.

What should I do after the IELTS test?

After the test, take a break before considering your next steps. Results normally arrive within a few days. Whatever the outcome, six weeks of structured preparation will have improved your English and revealed your remaining priorities; if you need a retake, you will be able to build a more focused IELTS study plan from the first attempt.

Official sources and references

  • ielts.org — official information and resources.
  • britishcouncil.org — official information and resources.

Six-week IELTS 7.0 plan

What is the weekly focus of this six-week plan?

This weekly split shows where to direct your available time while working towards IELTS 7.0 in six weeks. Use the earlier diagnostic to adjust these broad targets to your actual weaknesses.

WeekFocusTarget hours
1Diagnostic + right band needs2–3
2Listening and reading stamina10–12
3Writing task 2 drafting10–12
4Speaking fluency and part style8–10
5Full mock tests10–12
6Review, retest, calm routine6–8

faq.q: Can I really improve by a full band in six weeks?
faq.a: Moving from around 6 to 6.5 up to a 7 is realistic in six weeks with consistent, focused study and honest error analysis. Jumping two full bands, for example from 5 to 7, usually needs longer because it involves fundamental language growth, not just test technique.

faq.q: How many hours a day should I study for IELTS?
faq.a: Around 1.5 to 2 hours on weekdays plus a longer weekend block works well for most working applicants. Quality matters more than quantity: one hour of reviewing your mistakes is worth more than three hours of untargeted practice.

faq.q: Which section is hardest to improve quickly?
faq.a: Writing and Speaking usually improve the slowest because they depend on feedback and changing ingrained habits. Reading and Listening tend to rise faster because timed practice and error review produce quick, measurable gains.

faq.q: Should I take the Academic or General Training test?
faq.a: Almost all university and scholarship applicants need the Academic version. Confirm the exact requirement with your institution before booking, because the Reading and Writing sections differ between the two versions.

faq.q: Is it worth memorising sample answers?
faq.a: No. Examiners are trained to detect memorised responses, and using one that does not fit the specific question will lower your score. Learn flexible structures and vocabulary instead, so you can adapt to whatever question appears.

posts.title: TOEFL vs IELTS: Which English Test Should You Take?
posts.metaDescription: TOEFL vs IELTS compared: format, scoring, difficulty, cost, and acceptance. A clear guide to choosing the right English test for your goals.
posts.excerpt: A practical comparison of TOEFL vs IELTS covering format, scoring, difficulty, and acceptance, so you can confidently choose the test that plays to your strengths.
posts.bodyHtml:
What is the TOEFL vs IELTS decision, and why does it matter?

The TOEFL vs IELTS question is one of the first decisions international students face, and choosing well can save you time, money, and stress. Both tests measure academic English and both are accepted by thousands of universities worldwide, but they differ in format, style, and the type of candidate they suit. This guide breaks down the TOEFL vs IELTS comparison across everything that actually matters so you can pick the test that plays to your strengths rather than fighting against them.

Is one of the two tests universally easier?

There is no universally easier test. The right answer depends on your English background, how you handle a computer versus a face-to-face examiner, and what your target institutions accept. Let us work through it methodically.

Key takeaways

If you only have thirty seconds, these are the answers that decide most TOEFL vs IELTS outcomes.

  • Both TOEFL and IELTS are widely accepted; always confirm what your specific programme requires first.
  • The core TOEFL vs IELTS difference is style: TOEFL is fully computer-based and American-leaning, while IELTS Academic offers a human Speaking examiner.
  • TOEFL Speaking is recorded into a microphone; IELTS Speaking is a live conversation, which suits different personalities.
  • IELTS uses a 0 to 9 band scale; TOEFL iBT is scored out of 120.
  • Choose based on your strengths, comfort with technology, and destination, not on rumours about difficulty.

The basics of each test

What is the TOEFL iBT?

The TOEFL iBT is produced by ETS and is delivered almost entirely online, either at a test centre or at home. It leans towards North American English and academic contexts, with lecture-style listening passages and integrated tasks that combine skills.

What is the IELTS?

The IELTS is jointly run by the British Council, IDP, and Cambridge. The Academic version, which most applicants take, uses a mix of British and international English. Its defining feature is a face-to-face Speaking test with a real examiner, which no other major test offers in the same way.

Who accepts which test

Acceptance is rarely the deciding factor anymore because the vast majority of universities in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and Europe accept both. That said, some specific programmes, professional bodies, or immigration routes prefer one. The golden rule in any TOEFL vs IELTS decision is to check the exact requirement for your target course before you book anything.

Format and structure compared

Both tests assess Reading, Listening, Writing, and Speaking, but the experience of each differs meaningfully.

How does the Reading section differ?

TOEFL Reading uses long academic passages with multiple-choice questions, all on screen. IELTS Academic Reading offers a wider variety of question types, including matching headings, True/False/Not Given, and sentence completion, which some candidates find more varied and others find fiddly.

How does the Listening section differ?

TOEFL Listening features university lectures and campus conversations, and you take notes then answer afterward. IELTS Listening includes everyday and academic scenarios, and you answer as you listen, which rewards candidates who process information in real time.

How does the Writing section differ?

TOEFL Writing includes an integrated task, where you read, listen, then write a response combining both sources, plus an independent essay. IELTS Academic Writing has Task 1, describing a chart, graph, or process, and Task 2, an opinion or argument essay. If you dislike interpreting data visuals, that IELTS Task 1 is worth weighing carefully.

How does the Speaking section differ?

This is the sharpest difference in the whole TOEFL vs IELTS comparison. TOEFL Speaking is delivered by speaking into a microphone, with your responses recorded and scored later, sometimes partly by automated systems. IELTS Speaking is a live, three-part conversation with a human examiner. Introverts and those who freeze when recorded often prefer the human interaction of IELTS, while people who dislike being watched sometimes prefer the privacy of the TOEFL microphone.

Scoring: understanding the two scales

How is the IELTS scored?

IELTS reports each section and an overall score on a 0 to 9 band scale, in half-band increments. Most competitive universities ask for an overall 6.5 to 7.5, often with minimums in each section.

How is the TOEFL scored?

TOEFL iBT scores each section from 0 to 30, giving a total out of 120. Typical requirements sit around 80 to 100 for many programmes, with more selective courses asking for higher. Because the scales are so different, it helps to convert your target university requirement into both systems before deciding, so you know which score feels more attainable for you.

Which test is easier?

Is TOEFL easier than IELTS?

There is no honest single answer, but there are patterns. TOEFL tends to suit candidates who are comfortable with academic, lecture-heavy content, typing quickly, and working entirely on a computer for several hours. Its question types are more predictable and repetitive, which some learners find easier to drill.

Is IELTS easier than TOEFL?

IELTS tends to suit candidates who prefer variety, who write comfortably by hand or on screen, and who perform better talking to a real person. Its wider range of question types can feel less monotonous, though it means more formats to master.

Ask yourself one question: do I perform better speaking to a human being or to a microphone? Your honest answer settles the Speaking section, which is where many candidates gain or lose the most.

Practical factors: cost, availability, and results

How much do TOEFL and IELTS cost?

Pricing for both tests is broadly comparable and varies by country, so check current local fees rather than relying on old figures. Availability also depends on where you live; in some regions IELTS has more test dates and centres, in others TOEFL is easier to book, including its at-home option.

How fast will I get my results?

Results turnaround is fast for both, typically within a couple of weeks, and both offer computer-delivered IELTS options in many locations that speed things up. If you are on a tight application deadline, availability and result speed in your specific city may matter more than any format preference.

How to make your decision

What steps should I follow to decide?

Work through these steps in order. First, confirm which tests your target universities and any funders accept, and note the exact score required. Second, take a free sample or diagnostic of each test to feel the difference directly rather than relying on rumours. Third, weigh your personal strengths: comfort with technology, handwriting versus typing, and human versus recorded Speaking. Fourth, check practical logistics of cost and test dates in your area.

Can a tool help me map my requirement to a realistic target?

If your English level is borderline for the score you need, our AI advisor can help you interpret each university requirement and map it to a realistic target. Once you know which test suits you, you can also use our results tool to find scholarships and programmes that accept your chosen test.

TOEFL vs IELTS: Which English Test Should You Take?: what this guide covers

What does this guide cover for a Pakistani student?

This guide explains everything a Pakistani student needs to know about TOEFL vs IELTS, including eligibility, costs, timelines and practical steps. Use the sections above to find the exact information you need, or bookmark this page and return as your application progresses. Each answer below is written as a standalone question so you can jump straight to the detail you are stuck on, from basic eligibility through to fees, booking and the final registration decision.

A quick decision summary

Should I choose TOEFL or IELTS?

Lean towards TOEFL if you are comfortable with computers, American-style academic content, typed essays, and speaking into a microphone, or if your destination is primarily North America. Lean towards IELTS if you prefer variety in question types, a live human Speaking examiner, and if you are heading to the UK, Australia, or many European programmes. In the end, the best result in the TOEFL vs IELTS debate comes from choosing the test that fits how you naturally perform, then preparing thoroughly for it.

How Your English Learning Background Affects the TOEFL vs IELTS Decision

What is TOEFL vs IELTS 2026?

In 2026 both exams are unchanged in structure from recent years: the TOEFL iBT remains a fully computer-delivered, four-section test scored out of 120, and IELTS Academic remains a paper or computer test scored on a 0 to 9 band with a separate face-to-face Speaking session. What has shifted is availability. Computer-delivered IELTS and TOEFL at-home options now run in more Pakistani cities than before, so the TOEFL vs IELTS decision is increasingly driven by format fit and booking availability rather than by anything that has changed on the page.

Does an English-medium education change the result?

One of the most overlooked factors in choosing between TOEFL and IELTS is the way you learned English. Students who studied in English-medium schools, consumed English media regularly, and practised academic writing in English tend to perform differently on each test compared to students who learned English primarily through formal classroom instruction.

What if I learned English in an Urdu-medium classroom?

If your education was entirely in English, you likely have strong listening and reading comprehension skills developed through exposure to lectures, textbooks and media in English. These students often perform well on the TOEFL listening section, which requires you to understand extended academic lectures and answer questions about their structure and content. The TOEFL listening format rewards sustained attention and the ability to follow a single speaker for several minutes.

Which test suits a formal classroom learner better?

Students who learned English more formally, perhaps through Urdu-medium schooling with English as a second language, may find the IELTS format more familiar and comfortable. IELTS uses a wider variety of English accents, including British, Australian and occasionally New Zealand English. The IELTS reading section also uses a wider variety of text types, including advertisements, newspaper articles and book extracts, rather than exclusively academic passages.

How does Speaking differ for a cautious speaker?

The speaking section is where the difference is most pronounced. The TOEFL speaking section is entirely recorded and timed, which suits students who are comfortable speaking into a microphone but who may feel nervous in a live interaction. The IELTS speaking section involves a face-to-face conversation with an examiner, which suits students who thrive on human interaction and who can adjust their responses based on the examiner follow-up questions.

Is the Writing section different too?

The writing section differences are subtler. TOEFL writing requires you to integrate information from a reading passage and a lecture in one task. IELTS writing Task 1 requires you to describe and analyse visual information such as graphs, charts or diagrams. If you are strong at data interpretation, IELTS Task 1 plays to your strengths. If you are stronger at synthesising written and spoken information, the TOEFL integrated task may be more comfortable.

What does TOEFL vs IELTS cover?

Whatever path brought you to this decision, be honest with yourself about your actual skill profile before you commit to a test. Students who spent years in English-medium classrooms often assume the reading and writing sections need little preparation, only to discover that both tests grade style and formats they have never practised, while students from Urdu-medium backgrounds sometimes avoid the speaking test unnecessarily when regular spoken English is already part of their routine.

So which test should I actually trust to decide?

The reliable test is not your intuition but one full-length practice exam of each type, scored under timed conditions, and the result of those two sessions should decide more than any amount of general advice. Preparation time is real and limited, and it is best spent matching your strengths to the test that rewards them most.

TOEFL vs IELTS Preparation Strategies: What to Focus on for Each Test

Do TOEFL and IELTS need different preparation?

Preparing for the TOEFL and preparing for the IELTS require different strategies, even though both tests measure the same underlying English proficiency. The most efficient preparation plan understands the specific demands of each test and targets your preparation accordingly.

What is the highest-impact TOEFL preparation?

For TOEFL preparation, the single highest-impact activity is practising with full-length official practice tests under timed conditions. The TOEFL is a long test, approximately three hours, and stamina matters as much as language skill. Take at least three to four full-length practice tests in the weeks before your exam, simulating real test conditions. Pay particular attention to the integrated tasks, which combine reading, listening and writing, as these are unique to TOEFL.

Which TOEFL vs IELTS tips actually work?

For IELTS preparation, focus on understanding the specific format of each section. In the listening section, you hear each recording only once and have a short time to transfer answers, so practising quick note-taking is essential. In the reading section, the question types vary significantly, including matching headings, sentence completion, true or false statements and multiple choice. Familiarise yourself with every question type and develop a reliable strategy for each one.

What are the TOEFL vs IELTS requirements?

Vocabulary preparation differs between the two tests. TOEFL tends to use more academic vocabulary, which means building familiarity with academic word lists is worthwhile. IELTS vocabulary requirements are broader and more varied, including everyday language, idiomatic expressions and collocations that appear in the speaking and writing sections. Reading widely in English is one of the most effective ways to build vocabulary for either test.

How should I manage time in each test?

Time management during the test is a critical skill for both exams but manifests differently. TOEFL gives you a fixed time for each section and does not allow you to move between sections. IELTS allows some flexibility within sections, particularly in reading and writing. Practising under timed conditions for both tests helps you develop the pacing instincts that prevent you from running out of time on any section.

How do you apply for TOEFL vs ielts?

Daily preparation works because each test rewards consistent, low-stakes exposure more than heroic sprints. Twenty minutes a day of the right kind of practice, a TOEFL lecture transcript one day, an IELTS speaking preparation note in your own words the next, compounds quickly, and it is gentler than weekend marathons that cut into your other application work. When you review practice answers, focus on the patterns the examiner is actually looking for rather than the raw score: in writing, this means a clear position held throughout; in speaking, it means structure you can hear, not vocabulary you can count. Keep a small error log of the three or four recurring slips, and check each new practice test against that list, because fixing a handful of habits lifts scores faster than buying another book of exercises ever will.

What Each Test Actually Looks Like: Section-by-Section Walkthrough

Why walk through the structure before registering?

Understanding the concrete structure of each test helps you visualise what you will face on test day. The following walkthrough covers the key sections of both TOEFL and IELTS.

What does TOEFL Reading look like?

The TOEFL reading section presents three to four academic passages, each approximately seven hundred words long, followed by ten questions per passage. Passages are drawn from university-level textbooks across various disciplines. You have approximately fifty-four minutes for the entire reading section. The passages are dense and academic, and the questions require careful reading rather than skimming.

What does IELTS Reading look like?

The IELTS reading section contains three passages with a total of forty questions, and you have sixty minutes. The question types are more varied than TOEFL, including matching information, matching headings, labelling diagrams, summary completion, sentence completion, short-answer questions and multiple choice.

What is TOEFL vs ielts?

The TOEFL listening section consists of three to four lectures, each three to five minutes long, followed by two to three conversations. You hear each recording once and then answer questions. The entire listening section takes approximately thirty-six minutes.

What does IELTS Listening look like?

The IELTS listening section has four sections with ten questions each, totalling forty questions in thirty minutes. Section one is a conversation in an everyday context. Section two is a monologue on an everyday topic. Section three is a conversation in an academic context. Section four is an academic monologue. You hear each recording once, and you must transfer answers in the final ten minutes.

What TOEFL vs IELTS interview questions should you prepare for?

TOEFL speaking has four tasks combining independent responses with integrated tasks. IELTS speaking is a three-part face-to-face interview. TOEFL writing has an integrated task and an independent essay. IELTS writing has a task based on visual data and a discursive essay. Understanding these structures before preparation ensures that you practise effectively.

What else changes on test day?

Walking through the sections before you register does not cost practice time; it buys you confidence that saves far more. You learn, for example, that IELTS listening places all its questions in the order of the audio, while TOEFL allows you to take notes during lectures and answer afterwards, and those two mechanics reward opposite habits of attention. You also discover that the computer-based keyboard of the TOEFL essay and the longhand option of the IELTS essay are different physical tasks worth rehearsing once or twice, so that the writing itself never becomes part of the stress on the day. By the time the real test arrives, the format should feel familiar enough that the only variable left is the content, which is exactly where preparation belongs.

TOEFL vs IELTS Acceptance by Destination Country and University Type

Both TOEFL and IELTS are accepted by thousands of universities worldwide, but the degree of acceptance varies by destination country and institution type.

Which test do US universities accept?

In the United States, TOEFL has historically been the dominant test, but IELTS acceptance has grown significantly, and most US universities now accept both tests equally. For undergraduate and most graduate programs, either test is equally accepted, and your choice should be based on which test suits you better.

Which test should I take for the UK?

In the United Kingdom, IELTS has traditionally been the preferred test. The UKVI requires IELTS for visa purposes in certain categories. For Pakistani students targeting the UK, IELTS is the more natural choice, both because of its widespread acceptance and because the British accent used in the test is closer to what you will encounter in the UK.

What about Canada?

In Canada, both tests are accepted by virtually all universities and colleges. Canada immigration authorities accept both TOEFL and IELTS for study permit purposes. The choice should come down to personal preference and test format suitability.

Which test works best for Australia and New Zealand?

Australia and New Zealand strongly favour IELTS. While TOEFL is accepted by Australian universities, IELTS is more widely understood and is the default choice for most Australian applications. For students targeting Australia, IELTS is generally the more practical choice.

What if I am targeting Europe?

In Europe, where Germany, the Netherlands and Scandinavian countries have a growing number of English-taught programs, both tests are widely accepted. For Pakistani students considering multiple destinations, choosing IELTS gives you the broadest acceptance across the UK, Australia and Europe, while choosing TOEFL is most advantageous for US-focused applications.

What funding and benefits does TOEFL vs IELTS provide?

Treat the acceptance question as a programme-by-program fact rather than a country-wide generalisation, because the two tests trade advantages in ways that brochures cannot capture. A department that promises full funding may quietly prefer the TOEFL because the score report is machine-read by many US systems, while a UK university that publishes a single IELTS requirement for its international office will expect that number and no equivalent. Reading the exact wording on the official programme page for your field, not the international admissions page at the top of the website, settles the matter in five minutes and prevents the costly situation of presenting the wrong test after months of preparation.

Cost Breakdown and Scheduling Tips for Pakistani Test-Takers

Cost and scheduling are practical factors that can tip the decision between TOEFL and IELTS, particularly for students in Pakistan where test centre availability and pricing differ from other countries.

How much does the TOEFL cost in Pakistan?

The TOEFL iBT test fee in Pakistan is typically in the range of USD 185 to USD 250. The TOEFL is administered at certified test centres across Pakistan, including in Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad, Faisalabad and Peshawar. Book your test at least two to three months before your target date to ensure availability.

How much does the IELTS cost in Pakistan?

The IELTS test fee in Pakistan is typically in the range of PKR 48,000 to PKR 55,000 for the Academic module. IELTS is administered by the British Council and IDP, and test centres are available in most major cities. The computer-delivered version is offered more frequently, giving you more scheduling flexibility.

Can I get results faster or combine scores?

Both tests offer expedited results for an additional fee. TOEFL offers a MyBest score option, which combines your best scores from multiple test sessions. IELTS computer-delivered version delivers results within three to five days, compared to thirteen days for the paper-based version.

How much does TOEFL vs IELTS cost?

Additional costs include preparation materials, typically between PKR 3,000 and PKR 8,000, and preparation courses ranging from PKR 15,000 for an online course to PKR 50,000 or more for an intensive in-person programme. Sending scores to universities also incurs a fee: TOEFL allows four free score reports, with additional reports costing approximately USD 20 each. IELTS allows up to five free score reports. Factor these costs into your overall study-abroad budget.

What are the TOEFL vs IELTS deadlines and timeline?

Budget for the test as a project, not a single purchase, because the responsible plan includes a retake fund. Compare the registration fee in rupees, the centre distance and the waiting time for a result for your city, then add the cost of a second attempt and the price of an hour with a reputable speaking partner or a writing review. Booking the retake window in advance, even before you know whether you need it, protects both your schedule and your application deadlines, since a result that arrives two weeks late can be worthless to a university with a single cutoff. The small extra cost of planning for it is nearly always cheaper than negotiating after missing a scholarship deadline, so let the calendar, not optimism, decide when you sit again.

A Quick Decision Framework for Choosing Between TOEFL and IELTS

If you have read through the differences and are still uncertain which test to take, the following decision framework distils the key factors into a simple series of questions.

First question: where am I applying?

If your primary target is the United States, TOEFL gives you the widest acceptance. If your primary target is the United Kingdom, Australia or New Zealand, IELTS is the more natural choice. If you are applying to multiple countries, IELTS offers the broadest global acceptance.

Second question: how do I handle speaking tests?

If you are comfortable with a face-to-face conversation, IELTS speaking will likely feel natural. If you prefer speaking into a microphone with structured preparation time, TOEFL speaking may produce a higher score by removing that pressure.

Third question: how strong is my academic vocabulary?

TOEFL tends to use more academic vocabulary. If you have a strong academic vocabulary, TOEFL rewards that strength. If your English is strong but more general, IELTS may be more accessible.

Fourth question: how is my stamina?

TOEFL is a longer test, approximately three hours, with a single continuous session. IELTS is slightly shorter overall, and the speaking component is scheduled separately. If you find long tests exhausting, IELTS structure may help you perform better.

Fifth question: what is my timeline?

If you need results quickly, the computer-delivered IELTS delivers scores in three to five days. TOEFL scores are typically available within six to ten days.

Should I take a practice test of each before deciding?

Free official practice tests are available on both the ETS and British Council websites. Compare not just your scores but how you felt during each test. Your comfort level and performance on these practice tests are often the most reliable indicator of which test will produce your best real score.

How do I lock the decision in?

Once the mock results narrow the choice, resist the urge to keep comparing in circles and lock the decision in writing: test, target score, test date in three options, and the practice materials you will finish first. Set the decision rule now, for example, if the computerised TOEFL mock equals or beats the IELTS mock within target bands, the TOEFL gets the registration, and thereafter no more comparison shopping, only execution. A decision made once, rather than re-litigated every evening, preserves the energy that actually raises your score, and it leaves you free to convert the identical knowledge, grammar and vocabulary into the format the chosen test wants to see.

How Pakistani Students Typically Perform on TOEFL vs IELTS and Where to Focus

Patterns in how Pakistani test-takers perform on the two tests are useful signals, not guarantees. While every student is different, the consistent feedback from preparation centres and language teachers points to the same few areas where Pakistani candidates gain or lose marks on each exam.

What TOEFL vs IELTS tips should you follow?

In the IELTS listening section, Pakistani students often lose marks on the gap-filling and note-completion tasks because answers must be spelled correctly and within a word limit. Practice groups words such as dates, times and place names carefully, because errors there are marked wrong even when the meaning is clear. In the TOEFL listening section, the challenge for many Pakistani students is stamina: sustaining concentration across lectures that run several minutes long. Building sustained listening sessions into your preparation, rather than only short clips, is the most effective fix.

What should I do about reading vocabulary?

In the reading sections, vocabulary is the recurring issue. IELTS passages include a wider variety of text types, which suits students who read general English well, while TOEFL passages are strictly academic. If you read academic papers and textbooks regularly, the TOEFL passage style will feel familiar. If you read news and general non-fiction, IELTS gives you a more natural path. Build a vocabulary log of words you meet while reading and test yourself on them weekly, because passive recognition under timed conditions is what the test actually measures.

How do I handle the speaking section?

The speaking sections reward different habits. Pakistani candidates who learned English through formal grammar classes sometimes sound careful but slow, and in the IELTS face-to-face format, an examiner can prompt you, which helps. In the TOEFL recorded format, that prompting does not happen, and hesitation stands out more. Practice recording yourself on a phone and listening back for pauses, fillers and unfinished sentences. The goal is not perfect fluency but consistent, structured responses that stay on topic.

What should you write in your TOEFL vs IELTS essays?

In the writing sections, the difference is between argumentative and descriptive tasks. IELTS Task 1 turns graphs and charts into text, a skill that many students never practise because it does not appear in school writing. TOEFL integrated writing asks you to compare a reading passage with a lecture, which is closer to academic note-taking. Whichever test you choose, write at least two full timed essays per week and get feedback from a teacher or an online marking service, because self-practice without feedback can cement the same errors.

How do I find out which section is holding me back?

The most reliable way to know where you stand is to take one full timed practice test of each exam before deciding. Compare your section scores, and look at which sections lagged and by how much. Many students find the decision becomes obvious once they see the breakdown, because the test that fits their reading and stamina habits almost always scores higher.

Frequently Asked Questions About TOEFL vs IELTS

Students tend to repeat the same set of questions when choosing between the two tests, so the practical answers below address the most common ones directly.

Can I take both tests and submit the better score?

Yes, and some students do. If your applications are spread across countries, or if you simply want options, taking both is legitimate. The cost of preparation and the exam fees are the main drawbacks, so most students who try both take one first, see the result, and only take the second if the first is below the target for their chosen programs.

Which test is easier, TOEFL or IELTS?

Neither is universally easier. The answer depends on your speaking style, your vocabulary range and your stamina. Students who speak comfortably with a person usually find IELTS speaking easier. Students who prefer structured typing and recorded responses often find TOEFL more predictable. Take a practice test of each rather than relying on general opinions.

Are there differences in how universities view the two tests?

For admissions purposes, most universities in Canada, the US, the UK and Australia accept both and scale them against the same English proficiency standard. Where a difference appears is in the context of immigration: the UK and Australia use IELTS more commonly in their visa materials, while the US historically lists TOEFL more often. Neither fact closes any realistic door for you, but it can tip the choice if you have a primary destination.

How long do scores stay valid?

Both tests report that scores are valid for two years from the test date. Some universities interpret this as valid until the start of your program rather than the date of application, so a score taken more than a year before enrolment can be borderline. If your gap year is long and your first score is near your validity edge, retaking is usually easier than arguing for an exception.

What score do I actually need?

The requirement depends on your university and program. A common starting point is an overall band of 6.5 or 7.0 on IELTS, or roughly 90 to 95 on the TOEFL, for taught master programs across most English-speaking countries. Competitive programs ask for higher scores, and some set separate minimums for each section. Confirm the exact figures for each of your target programs and build a preparation target that clears the highest one by a small margin.

If I perform badly on one section, can I retake it?

Yes. Both ETS and the IELTS organisations allow you to retake the whole test as often as you like, and there is no limit on attempts. You report whichever sitting gives your best overall profile. On TOEFL, your best scores across multiple sittings can even be combined. Treat the first sitting as a realistic baseline and plan your retake date in advance, rather than deciding whether to retake only after seeing a disappointing score.
